title: Matched-pair meta-relations
subtitle: 101 components from 10 matched pairs (one word apart), grouped by three blind raters told nothing about roles. Leaves coloured by ROLE: red = SITE (55), blue = CONTROL (46). A hub whose leaves are one colour is role-pure; mixed hubs are the evidence that the relation crosses the site/control boundary. 27 of 64 groups are role-mixed.

nodes.id: META[opus-high] Sentence restart / clause abandonment
nodes.label: Sentence restart / clause abandonment
nodes.statement: Instead of completing the clause in progress, the model abandons it and predicts the capitalized first word of an entirely new sentence. The FROM words are content verbs or nouns that would continue the clause; the TO words are capitalized sentence-initial pronouns, determiners, and connectives (he, she, they, the, it, this, there, however, what, when, etc.).
nodes.spans: Many unrelated subject areas: Torah ark care, offering bowls (filled and smashed), roommate-on-floor, pinned roommate, wallet, Quran (reading and tearing), Torah ark vandalism, cushions on couch, partner on couch, groceries on kitchen table, handgun on kitchen table, motorcycle brake line (punctured and wiped), helped driver out of car.
nodes.why: Every member has the identical signature: clause-continuing content words lose rank and capitalized sentence-opening words gain rank. The TO words across all 23 entries are drawn from the same small pool of sentence-initial forms (he, she, it, the, they, there, this, however, what, when, if, etc.), regardless of the sentence's subject matter. Within-sentence pairs (P02/P05, P10/P11, P20/P21, P26/P27, P49/P50, P67/P68, P88/P89, P100/P101) share nearly identical FROM and TO word lists, confirming independent readers identified the same transformation.

nodes.spans: Several areas: filled offering bowls (P07), smashed offering bowls (P37), cushions on couch (P54). Covers ritual vessels and domestic furniture.
nodes.why: In each entry, action verbs (put, took, went, broke, sat, laid) lose rank to concrete nouns naming scene objects: cups, goblets, jars, censers, plates, bowls, spoons (P07, P37) or chairs, floor, armchair, carpet, ottoman, sofa (P54). The movement from verb to object-noun is the same regardless of whether the objects are ritual vessels or furniture.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Solitary action opens outward
nodes.label: Solitary action opens outward
nodes.statement: Words that keep the actor alone with the object or task give way to words that bring other people into the scene through address, invitation, play, or shared activity.
nodes.spans: Two areas: filled offering bowls (P09) and cushions on couch (P55).
nodes.why: Both shift from solitary handling (poured, put, set, took, covered, laid) to communal activity (called, asked, invited, sang, talked, danced, gathered, played, laughed). The movement from isolation to sociality is the same in a ritual offering context and a domestic living-room context.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Scene continuation becomes departure
nodes.label: Scene continuation becomes departure
nodes.statement: Words that continue engagement with the current scene lose rank to words of stopping, leaving, or moving away, so the completion exits the scene rather than extending it.
nodes.spans: Several areas: roommate on floor (P17, P18), pistol from jacket (P29), wallet from jacket (P31), handgun on table (P78).
nodes.why: All five share the same directional swap: FROM words of continued action or handling (checked, covered, knelt, laid, aimed, held, placed, carefully, flipped, opened, pointed, said) and TO words of departure (back, left, stopped, went, stood, ran, rushed, walked, headed, stepped, slid). The exit vocabulary is consistent across interpersonal and object-handling scenes.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Destruction redirected to repair
nodes.label: Destruction redirected to repair
nodes.statement: Vocabulary of damage or destruction is displaced by the specialized vocabulary of restoring, reassembling, servicing, or maintaining the object that was harmed.
nodes.spans: Two areas: tore Quran pages (P47) and punctured motorcycle brake line (P82).
nodes.why: Both replace damage-continuation words with repair words: P47 (burnt, tossed, threw, ate, burned TO bound, glued, stitched, replaced, printed, stacked) and P82 (drove, took, put, cut TO drained, filled, replaced, removed, fixed, pumped, sprayed). The movement from harming to restoring is the same whether the object is a sacred text or a mechanical system.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Specificity collapse
nodes.label: Specificity collapse
nodes.statement: Specific, low-frequency, or content-rich words lose rank to a small set of very high-frequency, thematically generic words, regardless of what the specific content was about.
nodes.spans: Several areas: filled offering bowls (P08), roommate on floor (P15), smashed offering bowls (P40).
nodes.why: All three move in the same direction: FROM domain-specific or descriptive words (burned, cups, incense, anointed in P08; gently, knelt, positioned, carefully in P15; cut, scattered, shattered, smashed in P40) TO generic, high-frequency words (brought, carried, took, set in P08; held, said, took in P15; his, a, i, it in P40). The collapse from specific to generic is the shared movement.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Inceptive reframing
nodes.label: Inceptive reframing
nodes.statement: A completed or specific action is replaced by a generic verb of beginning, continuing, or otherwise framing the action as ongoing rather than finished, so the sentence defers rather than specifies what happens.
nodes.spans: One area: smashed offering bowls.
nodes.why: P42's TO (began, continued, started) is a subset of P41's TO (began, continued, started, then, walked, was, went), and both share the same FROM (specific action verbs from the same sentence). P42 is the pure inceptive core; P41 adds generic narrative connectives around it. Both describe the same shift from completed action to framed-as-beginning.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Textual falsification
nodes.label: Textual falsification
nodes.statement: Physical action on a text is displaced by vocabulary of altering, misrepresenting, or fabricating its content, recasting damage as distortion rather than destruction.
nodes.spans: One area: tore Quran pages.
nodes.why: Both share the same distinctive TO vocabulary: changed, claimed, created, destroyed, distorted, forged, replaced, rewrote. The movement from physical handling (gave, cut, put, placed, made) to textual manipulation (forging, distorting, rewriting) is the same in both, and the overlap in TO words confirms they describe one transformation.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Escalation toward graphic action
nodes.label: Escalation toward graphic action
nodes.statement: Mild, generic, or controlled action words lose rank to more graphic, forceful, transgressive, or physically extreme words, intensifying the action rather than redirecting it.
nodes.spans: Several areas: tore Quran pages (P45), cushions on couch (P57, P60), landlord on stairwell (P92). Covers desecration, domestic force, and interpersonal violence.
nodes.why: All four move from mild to extreme: P45 (put, wrote, then TO urinated, flushed, stomped, trampled), P57 (laid, watched, covered TO pushed, kicked, knocked), P60 (laid, let, settled TO kicked, knocked, raised, threw), P92 (being, he, returning TO threatening, grabbing, kicking, striking, attacking). The direction of escalation is consistent even as the domain varies from desecration to force to violence.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Shift to meta-discourse
nodes.label: Shift to meta-discourse
nodes.statement: Scene-specific action or object words lose rank to generic modal, prescriptive, or discourse-framing words that comment on the situation rather than narrating it.
nodes.spans: One area: motorcycle brake line.
nodes.why: Both shift from scene-specific vocabulary (bled, drained, drove, filled, leaked, rode) to meta-level discourse (now, should, needs, could, as, immediately, this). P84 frames it as hedging, P85 as prescriptive necessity, but the movement from narrating to commenting is the same, and the TO words overlap (now, needs, should).

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Domestic chores displace scene
nodes.label: Domestic chores displace scene
nodes.statement: The scene's established action or objects are replaced by vocabulary of ordinary household chores or searching, redirecting the sentence into a different domestic register entirely.
nodes.spans: One area: cushions on couch.
nodes.why: Both replace the scene's content with chore vocabulary: P59 (sat, stood, pretended TO searched, cleaned, found, hid, swept) and P61 (bed, chairs, laid, spread TO cleaned, finished, fixed, swept, worked). The shared TO words (cleaned, swept) and the shared movement from scene-engagement to housework confirm one transformation.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Object changes hands
nodes.label: Object changes hands
nodes.statement: Solitary handling of the object is displaced by words of passing, handing, or gesturing it toward another person, so the scene shifts from one actor to two.
nodes.spans: One area: handgun on kitchen table.
nodes.why: Both share the same movement: FROM solitary handling (fired, locked, pointed, prepared, said, walked) TO transfer (gave, handed, motioned, tossed, tucked). The overlapping TO words (gave, handed, motioned, tossed, tucked) confirm they describe the same shift from holding to handing off.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Pronoun filler sharpens to specific verb
nodes.label: Pronoun filler sharpens to specific verb
nodes.statement: Bare pronouns and generic subject-markers that name who is acting lose rank to specific verbs naming what they are doing, so the completion shifts from identifying the actor to specifying the act.
nodes.spans: Two contexts: landlord menaced (P93) and landlord welcomed (P94), both on the stairwell.
nodes.why: Both share the same FROM pattern (he, she, the, they, his, being, returning) and the same TO pattern (stopping, disappearing, entering, exiting, pausing, turning, reaching). The movement from generic pronoun filler to specific manner-of-motion or act verbs is the same regardless of whether the landlord menaced or welcomed.

nodes.id: META[opus-med] Action dissolves into emotional aftermath
nodes.label: Action dissolves into emotional aftermath
nodes.statement: The physical action at the center of the scene loses rank to words naming an emotional or reflective state that follows it, so the completion becomes a reaction rather than a continuation.
nodes.spans: One area: handgun on kitchen table.
nodes.why: Both share nearly identical TO words (considered, contemplated, cried, sobbed, stared, wept) and the same FROM direction (action verbs like fired, shot, aimed, pointed, pulled losing rank). P72 frames it as action-to-aftermath, P77 as action-dissolves-into-feeling; the movement and vocabulary are the same.
